Still need to figure out why AR is not overwriting this method..

You are hitting a pretty unique combination of things...
1. Attribute methods (`#format` in this case since you have a column named "format") are lazily defined. Usually, the first time you call this method (e.g. BookFormat.first.format), it'll trigger method missing and define these methods on the class.
2. There's private method on `Kernel` (i.e. a "global" method) that takes at least one argument. Calling it with no arguments will raise the "too few arguments" error.
3. `as_json` and `to_json` uses `read_attribute_for_serialization` which is simply aliased to `send`.

Now, normally none of these are going to be a problem. Since `Kernel#format` is private, when first you call `BookFormat.first.format`, it'll trigger method missing as expected and define the (public) attribute methods, which overrides the private method from `Kernel` from thereon.

However, since `to_json` effectively just do a `BookFormat.first.send(:format)` it will reach the private method and causes the error.

A work around for your app for now is to make sure that those attribute methods are defined before you try to call `as_json`. The simplest way to do that with public API is to make sure `#format` is called at least once. 

We should fix this, but I'm unsure what's the best approach. We can switch `read_attribute_for_serialization` to use `public_send`, but doing this in a point release seems quite risky...

cc @josevalim @jeremy @rafaelfranca
(By the way, you probably shouldn't call `as_json` in your app. While it's a public API, this is more of a "hook method" intended for the encoder to consume.)

``` irb
>> bf.method(:format)
=> #<Method: BookFormat(Kernel)#format>
>> skip_backtrace { bf.send(:format) }
=> "#<ArgumentError: too few arguments>"
>> skip_backtrace { bf.send(:format) }
=> "#<ArgumentError: too few arguments>"
>> skip_backtrace { bf.send(:format) }
=> "#<ArgumentError: too few arguments>"
>> bf.method(:format)
=> #<Method: BookFormat(Kernel)#format>
>> bf.format
=> "paperback"
>> bf.method(:format)
=> #<Method: BookFormat(#<Module:0x007fe16d195a90>)#__temp__66f627d61647>
>> skip_backtrace { bf.send(:format) }
=> "paperback"
>> skip_backtrace { bf.send(:format) }
=> "paperback"
>> skip_backtrace { bf.send(:format) }
=> "paperback"
```

@chancancode I'm sorry, I don't understand what you mean by making sure #format is called at least once. We call as_json and extend it to add some more methods to it so the data is formatted correctly for the app that receives it.

I really don't know if I should be recommending this, but for example, if you split the line into this:

``` ruby

relation.first.try(:format)
relation.as_json
```

or even


The problem is I also have this line, which is the major issue:

```
  = f.input :format_id, label: 'Format', input_html: { id: 'book_format_tokens', data: { load: [@book.book_format].compact } }
```

That is for tokens so people can choose the format as they start typing and it performs a lookup so I can't use that trick.
I'm  also curious what changed between 4.0.4 and 4.1 to cause it to break.

@kakubei again, I feel stupid for recommending this, but you just have to call `#format` once at some point before your view code. Doing that will trigger the condition where the `BookFormat` class would go check its columns in the database and define the attribute methods once and for all. So as long as you do this once in your app sometime after the class is defined, you'll never see the problem again.

So I figured out the cause. It was working purely by accident in 4.0. This stopped working after https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/d1316bb128b1905995ba9f3e4ff35a628b845780#diff-1ecd313ff0ab827af30014553cf8918dL434.

The reason is that the code there used to call `respond_to?`, which is [another trigger point](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/master/activerecord/lib/active_record/attribute_methods.rb#L228) to generate the attribute methods. Presumably, that code path was executed when AR was trying to see if there's an `after_initialize` callback.

So, now that the code doesn't need to call `respond_to?` anymore after the refactor, things stopped working because of what I said earlier. :neutral_face:
